The character: verse 5 says he 'deals generously and lends,' verse 9 that he 'has distributed freely, and given to the poor' — the wealth in his house flows through it, not merely into it. And the psyche, priceless for an investor: 'he is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD' (v7). There is the finished product of this whole plan: a portfolio built by wisdom, held with open hands, on a generational clock, by a heart that no headline can stampede. Build toward the whole portrait — the balance sheet and the fearlessness both.
days.a: Set the generational clock: write investment goals in three horizons — 10 years (family provision), 30 years (children established), beyond (grandchildren and kingdom). Take one concrete step for the longest horizon today (a child's account, an estate conversation, a beneficiary update).
days.prayer: LORD, I want Psalm 112 — not just wealth in the house, but righteousness that endures, generosity that flows, offspring mighty in the land, and a heart unafraid of bad news. Build that whole portrait in me, asset by asset and year by year. Amen.
days.reflection: Which part of the Psalm 112 portrait are you furthest from — the wealth, the generosity, or the fearless heart? What does the generational clock change about this year's decisions?

verse.text: Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven... For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

days.teaching: Jesus was not anti-investment; He was anti-bad-investment. Read the Sermon's logic as an investor: earthly-only treasure has a fatal flaw in the fine print — moth, rust, thieves, and a terminal date; heavenly treasure is the only asset class with permanent returns. And He names the transfer mechanism plainly elsewhere: generosity — 'provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail' (Luke 12:33); giving is not the leak in your portfolio, it is the portion of it you've moved beyond the reach of every moth and market. Then the sentence that explains everything: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Your heart follows your money — invest in a company and you check its price; give to a mission and you start praying for it. So allocate deliberately, knowing your affections will follow the allocations. The fully-diagrammed biblical portfolio holds provision for your household, productive assets for the future, and a growing, joyful position in the one fund that survives you forever.
days.a: Make a heavenly allocation: alongside your investment contributions, set (or raise) a scheduled recurring gift to kingdom work you believe in — treated with the same seriousness, automation, and growth-rate as your investments. Watch where your heart goes next.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, audit my allocations. Let me hold earthly assets faithfully and heavenly ones passionately — moving treasure, month by month, where moth and rust and death have no claim. Take my money ahead of me, and let my heart follow it home. Amen.
days.reflection: Where does your treasure allocation say your heart is? What did you move today into the asset class that cannot fail?

verse.text: His master said to him, 'Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.'

days.teaching: The plan ends where it began — at the master's accounting — but now you can hear what the commended servants actually did, and gather the whole code: (1) You manage God's capital under mandate (Ps 24:1). (2) Multiplication is expected; burying is condemned (Matt 25). (3) Never hasten to be rich — farming, not gambling (Prov 28:20). (4) Divide portions among seven or eight (Eccl 11:2). (5) Invest only where knowledge has gone first (Prov 24:4). (6) Trust the harvest law — start early, contribute always, never dig up seed in a storm (Gal 6:9). (7) Move nothing major without counselors (Prov 11:14). (8) Kill expensive debt first; never borrow to invest (Prov 22:7). (9) Consider, then decide — buy productive fields, reinvest the fruit (Prov 31:16). (10) Define 'enough'; let giving outpace growing (1 Tim 6:9). (11) Sow on schedule regardless of clouds (Eccl 11:6). (12) Keep the heavenly allocation growing — it's the only permanent position (Matt 6:20). Write them into your Investment Policy Statement, sign it with your spouse or counselor as witness, and review it every January. Then go be boring, faithful, and free — until the day the Master says the only performance review that matters: well done.
days.a: Write your Investment Policy Statement: one page — the mandate (Day 2), your allocations and Joseph rate, the haste filter, the storm contract, your 'enough,' the counsel rule, the leverage ban, and the heavenly allocation. Sign it with a witness and calendar the annual review.
days.prayer: Master, I want the sentence the faithful servants heard. Take these twelve rules and burn them into my habits — faithful over a little, decade after decade, until You set me over much. The increase is Yours, the joy is Yours, and I intend to enter it. Amen.
days.reflection: Which of the twelve rules protects you from your particular weakness? What did it feel like to sign the policy — and who witnessed it?

plans.title: 14-Day Rules of Money
plans.tagline: The laws money obeys — ownership, sowing, debt, diligence, integrity, contentment, and account-giving.
plans.promise: Money follows laws as reliable as gravity, and Scripture wrote them down first. Fourteen days, fourteen rules — one per day, each applied the same day — until you stop fighting the laws of money and start building with them.

verse.text: The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein.

days.teaching: Every system of money management begins with an ownership claim, and Scripture's is total: the earth is the LORD's, and the fullness thereof. Haggai 2:8 sharpens it — 'The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, declares the LORD of hosts.' This is Rule 1 because every other rule collapses without it: if the money is yours, then budgeting is deprivation, giving is loss, saving is self-protection, and account-giving is nobody's business. If the money is God's, everything reverses — budgeting becomes management, giving becomes the Owner moving His resources, saving becomes assignment, and the audit becomes expected. The deepest financial problems are almost never arithmetic problems; they are lordship problems wearing arithmetic costumes. Settle the deed today and the next thirteen rules become executable. Skip it and they become tips — and tips have never changed anyone's life.
days.a: Transfer the title: write a one-line deed — 'Everything I have belongs to God; I am His manager' — and sign it. Then walk your home and accounts mentally, saying over each: 'His.' Notice which items resist the sentence; those are your idols' addresses.
days.prayer: LORD, the silver is Yours, the gold is Yours, the house and the accounts and the hands that earned them — Yours. I sign the deed today. Rule me before You rule my money, and make the next thirteen days a management briefing from my actual Owner. Amen.
days.reflection: Which possession or account resisted the word 'His'? What does that resistance tell you about where lordship hasn't reached?

days.t: Rule 2: You Can't Serve Two Masters

verse.text: No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.

days.teaching: Jesus' second rule is a job description: money makes an excellent employee and a merciless employer, and every person alive is in one of the two arrangements. He doesn't say you shouldn't serve both God and money; He says you cannot — the positions are mutually exclusive because each demands what the other forbids: money-as-master demands anxiety (v25 follows immediately: 'therefore do not be anxious'), hoarding, and compromise on command; God-as-master demands trust, generosity, and integrity that costs. The tell isn't your balance — rich people can serve God and poor people can serve money. The tell is who gives the orders: What do you think about unbidden? What can override your convictions? What do you consult before obeying God — the calling, the giving, the rest He commands? Mammon's employees get a paycheck of worry and a retirement of moths. Notice your master's voice today; you'll hear it around every decision that involves a number.
days.a: Track the master's voice for 24 hours: each time money drives a feeling or decision today (anxiety, comparison, a choice bent by cost), jot one word. Tonight, review the list and answer honestly: who was issuing orders today?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, only one throne, and money has been climbing on it. I fire the false master today. Take back the orders: my anxieties, my ambitions, my automatic calculations. Let money report to me, and let me report to You — one Master, freely chosen. Amen.
days.reflection: What did your 24-hour log reveal about who gives orders in your financial life? Where does money most successfully override your obedience?

verse.text: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.

days.teaching: Money obeys agriculture: output is proportional to planting, harvests arrive after delays, and seed eaten is harvest cancelled. Paul applies the law to generosity — sow bountifully, reap bountifully — and the whole of Scripture applies it everywhere else: diligent work sown now returns in seasons (Prov 12:11), skills sown in obscurity stand before kings later (Prov 22:29), money sown into productive assets compounds across years, and folly sown compounds too (Hosea 8:7 — sow wind, reap whirlwind). Two corollaries run most lives: first, everyone reaps — the only questions are what was planted and when it matures; the credit card is a harvest, and so is the pension. Second, seasons don't rush — the desperation move of digging up seed (cashing out, quitting early, abandoning the planted field) forfeits harvests at exactly the wrong time. Audit your current planting honestly: everything in your accounts, skills, and relationships ten years from now is being sown somewhere in this ordinary week.
days.a: Do the sowing audit: three columns — money, time, skills. Under each, write what you actually sowed last month. Then write the harvest each planting logically produces in 5-10 years. Change one planting today based on what you saw.
days.prayer: Lord of the harvest, I believe the law You wrote: I will reap what I'm sowing right now. Open my eyes to my real plantings — the noble and the careless — and give me the patience to sow bountifully in the fields that matter and wait for Your seasons. Amen.
days.reflection: What harvest currently growing in your life did you plant without thinking? What are you now sowing deliberately?

days.t: Rule 4: The First Portion Is Holy

verse.text: Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house. And thereby put me to the test, says the LORD of hosts, if I will not open the windows of heaven for you and pour down for you a blessing until there is no more need.

days.teaching: Rule 4 sets money's order of operations: the first portion goes back to God — first, not last; percentage, not leftovers. From Abel's firstborn offering to Israel's firstfruits to Proverbs 3:9 ('honor the LORD... with the firstfruits of all your produce'), the pattern is consistent, and Malachi adds something found nowhere else in Scripture: a divine dare — test me in this. Giving first does three things no other financial act can. It breaks money's spell at the exact moment of income (the first swing of the axe fells the idol before it settles in). It declares in cash — the world's most honest language — that God is actually first. And it enrolls you in the economy of windows: God's math, where nine-tenths under blessing goes further than ten-tenths under self-management — a claim the Owner invites you to verify experimentally. Whether your conviction is the tithe or grace-giving that meets or exceeds it, the rule stands: the first slice is holy. Structure it first and everything downstream inherits the order.
days.a: Move giving to first position: restructure your payday flow so your gift to God's work transfers first — before saving, before bills, automatically. If you've never tithed, take Malachi's test explicitly for 90 days and keep notes.
days.prayer: LORD of hosts, You asked to be tested — so I take the test. The first portion is Yours from today: first in order, first in honor. Break money's spell at my income's front door, and open whatever windows You choose. I'll keep honest notes. Amen.
days.reflection: What has kept giving in last place in your cash flow? What do you expect the 90-day test to show — and what would it mean if God passes it?

days.t: Rule 5: The Borrower Is the Slave

verse.text: The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender.

days.teaching: Rule 5 is the one modern economies are built on hoping you won't read: debt is not a product, it is a relationship — and Scripture names the relationship with an unsentimental word: slavery. The borrower's future labor is pre-sold; his income arrives pre-claimed; his options narrow to what the payments permit. That's not a metaphor — ask anyone whose calling, generosity, or family decisions are governed by what they owe. Scripture never calls borrowing sin, but it never once calls it blessing either: it consistently frames lending-freedom as strength (Deut 28:12 — 'you shall lend... and you shall not borrow') and debt as a condition to escape, urgently (Prov 6:1-5 — free yourself 'like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter'). The rule's applications: consumer debt for depreciating things is wealth-destruction on installment; every dollar of interest paid is a dollar sown into someone else's harvest; and freedom — not the payment being 'manageable' — is the goal. The gazelle doesn't negotiate a manageable relationship with the snare.
days.a: Face the ledger: list every debt — balance, rate, payment, and what it purchased. Total the monthly interest: that's your slavery bill. Then pick your escape method (avalanche or snowball), name the first target, and strike it with an extra payment today, even a small one.
days.prayer: Father, I've signed myself into servitudes You never assigned. Give me the gazelle's urgency. Let me hate the chains politely marketed to me, pay what I owe with integrity, and fight my way to the freedom where my labor answers to You alone. Amen.
days.reflection: What is your total monthly interest — your slavery bill? What could God do with that money, and with your freedom, once it's recovered?

verse.text: A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich.

days.teaching: Before any rule about managing money comes the rule about making it: wealth's ordinary source is diligent work — not luck, not leverage, not inheritance: the hand. Proverbs repeats it relentlessly: the diligent hand rules (12:24), the sluggard craves and gets nothing while the diligent soul is richly supplied (13:4), all hard work brings profit but mere talk leads to poverty (14:23). Scripture's economy runs on value creation: you serve people well, and money is the receipt. This dignifies every honest trade and exposes every wealth-without-work fantasy — the lottery culture, the passive-income mirage sold in courses, the speculation that produces nothing. It also points the ambitious at the true lever: your earning power is your largest financial asset, and it compounds through skill — 'do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings' (22:29). The diligent don't just work hard; they sharpen the axe — learning, improving, becoming more valuable per hour. Slack hands wait for money. Diligent hands go make some.
days.a: Sharpen the axe: identify the one skill that most increases your value to the people you serve, and take a concrete step today — enroll, practice, ask for the harder assignment, or schedule the certification. Also: name and kill one 'wealth without work' fantasy you've been feeding.
days.prayer: Father, You work, and You made my hands to work. Kill the slack in me — the corner-cutting, the fantasy of unearned ease. Make me diligent, skillful, and genuinely useful to the people You've placed in front of me, and let profit come the honest way. Amen.
days.reflection: Is your income problem actually a diligence or skill problem in disguise? What's the one skill that would most raise your service — and what did you do about it today?

days.t: Rule 7: False Scales Are an Abomination

verse.text: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight.

days.teaching: God polices weights and measures personally. 'Abomination' — Scripture's strongest disgust-word — lands not on some exotic wickedness but on crooked commerce: the rigged scale, the thumb on the balance. Rule 7: money gained by any dishonesty is cursed cargo. Proverbs tracks its trajectory — 'bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel' (20:17); 'the getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death' (21:6). The modern scales are subtler than the marketplace balance: the padded invoice and inflated expense report, the undisclosed defect, the résumé's convenient fictions, the cash job the tax return never met, the fine print designed to deceive, the hours billed but not worked. The rule cuts both ways: integrity costs money in the short run — that's what makes it integrity — and just weights are His delight, a word Scripture reserves for things close to God's heart. Every honest transaction is worship with a receipt. And a clean fortune, however small, sleeps better than a padded one ever has.
days.a: Calibrate your scales: audit your money-making honestly — pricing, invoices, taxes, hours, claims, disclosures. Find anything with a thumb on it and correct it today, even at cost. If restitution is owed (Zacchaeus-style), start it.
days.prayer: Righteous LORD, You weigh my weights. Expose every thumb I've laid on a scale — the rationalized, the customary, the 'everyone does it.' I choose the just weight and the smaller, cleaner gain. Delight in my ledgers, God, whatever the correction costs me. Amen.
days.reflection: Where has your integrity been quietly discounted for money? What did the correction cost — and what did it buy?

days.t: Rule 8: Plans Are Established by Counsel

verse.text: Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war.

days.teaching: Money decisions are war decisions — Solomon's own analogy — and Rule 8 forbids fighting them alone. The reason is diagnostic, not procedural: 'the heart is deceitful above all things' (Jer 17:9), and nowhere does it perform better than around money, where desire hires the intellect as its defense attorney. You don't see your blind spots — that is what makes them blind — but a counselor standing two feet to the side sees them instantly: the house you can't quite afford framed as 'stretching in faith,' the shiny investment framed as 'opportunity,' the resignation framed as 'calling' the same week you got a bad review. Scripture's standard is structural: many advisers (Prov 15:22), consulted before commitment, chosen for wisdom rather than agreement. In practice, three seats: someone competent in the domain, someone who knows your patterns, someone with zero stake who'll say the unwelcome sentence. And one law that makes the bench real: big decisions wait for the bench — an imposed 72-hour-plus-counsel delay on any major money move. The heart's best trick is urgency. Counsel is how God de-fangs it.
days.a: Adopt the war council rule in writing: 'No financial decision above $____ without 72 hours and counsel from my three.' Set your threshold, name your three seats, and apply the rule retroactively to anything currently pending.
days.prayer: Father, my heart argues its own case brilliantly and I keep losing to it. Give me a war council: wise, unbought, and unafraid of me. And give me the humility to wait for them — because the urgent whisper is almost never You. Amen.
days.reflection: What was your last major money decision made alone and fast — and how did it age? What threshold and three names did you write down?

verse.text: Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.

days.teaching: Rule 9 is money's law of velocity: wealth's durability is inversely proportional to the speed of its arrival. Fast money — windfalls, jackpots, sudden liquidity, speculation hits — dwindles, and not by bad luck: money that outruns the owner's character has nothing to hold onto; the lottery-winner bankruptcy statistics are Proverbs 13:11 wearing a lab coat. Slow money — gathered little by little — grows the gatherer along with the pile: each small deposit trains judgment, patience, and immunity to schemes, so that by the time the sum is large, the steward is large enough to hold it. This is why Scripture attacks every hurry-up scheme at the root: 'an inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end' (20:21); the one who hastens to be rich 'will not go unpunished' (28:20). The rule's daily application is a question asked of every financial opportunity: is this gathering, or grabbing? Gathering compounds. Grabbing dwindles. And if a windfall ever does find you — inheritance, bonus, sale — Rule 9's corollary: park it, wait 90 days, and let character catch up before the money moves.
days.a: Classify your money-making activities: label each current pursuit 'gathering' (slow, understood, compounding) or 'grabbing' (fast, opaque, adrenalized). Exit or downsize one 'grab' today. Write the windfall rule where you'll find it when you need it: '90 days parked before it moves.'
days.prayer: Lord, make me a gatherer in a culture of grabbers. Grow my character at the pace of my accounts, so that whatever You entrust arrives to hands that can hold it. And guard me from the hurry that You have promised to punish. Amen.
days.reflection: Which of your pursuits is honestly a 'grab'? Has money ever outrun your character — and what did it cost?

verse.text: Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you.'

days.teaching: Rule 10 is the only rule that caps the whole system, because without it no amount ever arrives: contentment. Hebrews welds it to a promise — be content, for He has said 'I will never leave you nor forsake you' — exposing what discontent actually is: not ambition, but quiet unbelief that God's presence plus present provision equals enough. The economics of the rule are staggering. Discontent is expensive: it is the engine of lifestyle inflation, upgrade cycles, comparison purchases, and the moving finish line that devours every raise. Contentment is income: Paul calls godliness with contentment 'great gain' (1 Tim 6:6) — the contented family lives richly on what dooms the discontented one to strain. And it must be learned — Paul's word (Phil 4:11-12): 'I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content,' schooled in both abundance and need. The curriculum is daily: gratitude spoken specifically, comparison starved deliberately (mute the feeds that manufacture wanting), and the promise rehearsed — He never leaves. The discontented person is poor on any income. The contented one is rich on nearly any. Same numbers. Different gods.
days.a: Starve comparison, feed gratitude: unfollow/mute your three worst 'wanting-manufacturers' today, and start a nightly three-item specific gratitude practice with your household. Then find one place to say the radical sentence: 'What I have is enough.'
days.prayer: God who never leaves, teach me the learned secret. Silence the voices that manufacture my wanting, and tune me to what You've already given. Let contentment be my gain, my raise, and my rest — because the promise is better than the upgrade. Amen.
days.reflection: What manufactures your wanting most reliably? Where did saying 'enough' out loud feel most costly — and most true?

verse.text: One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want. Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered.

days.teaching: Rule 11 is money's strangest law — the one that shouldn't work on paper: giving enriches; withholding impoverishes. Scattering that increases contradicts arithmetic but not agriculture: seed scattered is seed multiplied; seed clutched in the barn is seed lost to mold. Scripture stacks the testimony without embarrassment: the one who waters will be watered; 'give, and it will be given to you... pressed down, shaken together, running over' (Luke 6:38); 'whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed' (Prov 19:17) — the poor man's IOU co-signed by God. The mechanism is partly visible (generosity builds trust, relationships, and open doors; givers become people others delight to bless) and partly pure providence — windows, not formulas. Two guardrails keep the rule honest: give to bless, not to transact (the reward chases the giver who isn't chasing it), and give first-and-scheduled, not leftover-and-someday (Rule 4's order). The withholder's fate is the rule's dark half: hoarded resources 'suffer want' — of joy, of purpose, of the very security the hoarding sought. Water something today. Then watch the strange law work over years, not weeks.
days.a: Scatter deliberately today: give something that costs you — money to a need you've been aware of, a generous tip, an anonymous bill paid, time to someone with nothing to offer back. Then build one new scheduled generosity into your monthly flow.
days.prayer: Generous Father, You scattered Your own Son for me — teach me the law You live by. Make me a waterer: free-handed, cheerful, and unafraid of the math. Break the withholding instinct that promises safety and delivers want. I'd rather be Your river than my own reservoir. Amen.
days.reflection: Where has withholding cost you more than giving ever did? What did today's scattering do to the giver?

days.t: Rule 12: Provide for Your Own Household

verse.text: But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

days.teaching: Rule 12 grounds all the soaring rules in a floor of iron: provision for your own household is a faith-level obligation — Paul's language ('denied the faith, worse than an unbeliever') is the strongest he ever attaches to a money behavior. Provision is the first claim on your earning after God's portion: food, shelter, protection, and the forward-looking kinds Scripture models — training children in skill and wisdom, the Proverbs 31 household that 'is not afraid of snow' because provision was made in advance, the inheritance horizon of 13:22. Note what the rule sanctifies: the unglamorous paycheck. The believer grinding an ordinary job to keep a family fed is performing 1 Timothy 5:8, which is to say, practicing the faith — no mission trip required. Note also what it rebukes: spiritualized neglect (ministry or 'faith' language covering a family unfed, uninsured, or unplanned-for) and its opposite twin, provision inflated into a god that justifies absentee workaholism — the family needs presence provided too. The rule's modern checklist writes itself: income secured, essentials budgeted, insurance honest, the will written, the household's tomorrow considered. Unromantic, unphotographed — and 'worse than an unbeliever' is the grade for skipping it.
days.a: Run the provision audit: five checks — (1) household essentials covered by stable income? (2) life/health insurance adequate? (3) will and guardianship written? (4) emergency reserve funded? (5) presence — does your family get you, not just your paycheck? Fix the weakest item starting today.
days.prayer: Father, You feed sparrows and You've assigned me a household. Make me a provider in full — bread and presence, today's table and tomorrow's shelter. Keep me from neglect wearing spiritual clothes, and from work that feeds the family while starving it. Amen.
days.reflection: Which of the five provision checks is weakest? Is your household getting provision AND presence — or one disguised as both?

verse.text: A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous.

days.teaching: Rule 13 sets money's time horizon: two generations past your own funeral. The good man of Proverbs plans for grandchildren — deliberately accumulating, protecting, and transferring blessing that outlives him. This is the rule that turns all the others into architecture: margin (Rule for saving), multiplication (investing), provision (household) — compounded across a horizon long enough to change a family line's trajectory: the first debt-free generation, the first business owned, the first children educated without chains. But Scripture is clinical about inheritance's danger: wealth transferred without wisdom detonates — 'an inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end' (20:21), and Ecclesiastes groans over leaving wealth to 'the one who comes after me... and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool?' (2:18-19). So the rule has two ledgers, and the second is senior: leave treasure AND transmit the treasury code — children taught the fourteen rules are the only safe vault for the fourteen rules' proceeds. Practically: build assets that outlive you, write the will that directs them, and run the dinner-table academy that makes the transfer safe. Trees planted for shade you'll never sit in — that's the rule. It's also just love, with a longer clock.
days.a: Open the generational file: (1) write/update your will and beneficiaries, (2) start or fund one asset explicitly tagged for the next generation, (3) hold the first 'family treasury' conversation — teach one rule from this plan to your children or a young person you're investing in.
days.prayer: Father of generations, stretch my clock. Let me plant for shade I'll never sit in — assets that bless, and wisdom that guards the assets. Write my name among the good ancestors, and let my children's children find both the treasure and the map. Amen.
days.reflection: What trajectory-change could your family line experience if you executed this rule for 30 years? Which transfer are you most behind on — the treasure or the wisdom?

days.t: Rule 14: You Will Give an Account

verse.text: So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.

days.teaching: The final rule is the one that makes all the others matter: the audit is real. Each of us will give an account — and Jesus' money parables insist the account includes the ledgers: the talents reviewed line by line (Matt 25:19, 'settled accounts'), the manager summoned — 'give an account of your management' (Luke 16:2), the rich fool audited at midnight (Luke 12:20). Money, Jesus taught, is the training currency: 'if then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches?' (Luke 16:11) — every dollar handled is a rehearsal being graded for larger trusts. This rule is not terror; for the steward it is dignity: your budgeting, giving, saving, providing, and multiplying are seen, remembered, and headed for commendation — 'well done' is a real sentence God intends to say. So close the plan the way the audited close a quarter: review the fourteen rules, note where the books are clean and where they need correction, and set the annual review that keeps you audit-ready. Live ready to give the account. Then the accounting day — money's most avoided rule — becomes the day you've quietly been preparing for all along.
days.a: Hold the pre-audit: score yourself 1-10 on each of the fourteen rules, honestly. Pick your two lowest scores and write a 90-day correction plan for each. Calendar an annual 'account day' — same date every year — to re-score and adjust. Then teach the fourteen rules to one person.
days.prayer: Righteous Judge and generous Father, I will stand in Your audit — so I choose to live audit-ready. Thank You for every rule You wrote down in advance. Correct my books now, in mercy, so that day holds no terror — only the sentence I long to hear: well done. Amen.
days.reflection: If the account were tonight, which rules would shine and which would shame? What did you put in the 90-day correction plan — and who will learn the rules from you?

plans.title: 14-Day Generous Life
plans.tagline: Kingdom generosity — tithing, radical giving, and wealth that flows: the final purpose of every other money plan.
plans.promise: Fourteen days on money's true endgame: giving as worship, the tithe and beyond, secret generosity, hospitality, kingdom investing, and building a family that gives for generations — until open hands become your resting position.

days.t: God So Loved That He Gave

verse.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.

days.teaching: The Bible's most famous verse is a giving verse: God so loved that He GAVE — and gave His most precious, not His surplus. Generosity is not one Christian virtue on a long list; it is the family resemblance — the single trait that makes you look most like the Father whose defining act was donation. This reframes the entire plan before a dollar moves: giving is not fundraising, obligation, or losing money slower — it's imitation ('be imitators of God, as beloved children... as Christ loved us and GAVE himself up for us,' Eph 5:1-2), it's the cure for money's grip (every act of giving is a small exorcism of mammon), and it's joy's strangest doorway ('it is more blessed to give than to receive' — Jesus' only saying preserved outside the Gospels, Acts 20:35, as if the early church couldn't afford to lose that one). The generous life is the endgame of every other wealth plan you've done: you got out of debt, learned to earn, save, and invest — FOR THIS. Rivers, not reservoirs. Start by settling the destination.
days.a: Give something today — immediately, before the plan teaches you anything else: money, a meal, an hour, a possession someone admired. Not strategically. Just practice the family resemblance once, and notice what it does in you.
days.prayer: Father, You so loved that You gave — Your best, not Your extra. Make giving my family resemblance. Over these fourteen days, pry my fingers open joint by joint, until open hands are my resting position. Amen.
days.reflection: What did the immediate, unstrategic gift do in you? What do you currently believe giving costs you — and what does John 3:16 say it expresses?

days.t: The Cheerful Giver — Heart Before Amount

verse.text: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

days.teaching: Before amounts, God addresses the giver's face: not reluctantly (grudging generosity is taxation with religious paperwork), not under compulsion (manipulated giving profits the manipulator, not the soul), but as DECIDED in the heart — deliberate, free, and cheerful (Paul's Greek is hilaron; hilarious giving — God loves a giver who finds it FUN). This day rearranges motives before the plan rearranges budgets. The wrong engines: guilt (gives until the feeling stops), pressure (gives while watched), transaction (gives to obligate God — the prosperity distortion that turns generosity back into acquisition with extra steps). The right engine, per the chapter: grace experienced becoming grace extended — Paul's exhibit is the Macedonians (2 Cor 8:1-4), whose 'abundance of joy and extreme poverty overflowed in a wealth of generosity,' BEGGING for the privilege of giving. Poverty plus joy equals begging to give: that equation only balances when giving is understood as gain — participation in what God is doing, the 'grace of giving' as literal grace. Check your engine today. Cheerfulness isn't the entry requirement (start where you are); it's the destination the right engine reaches.
days.a: Run the engine check: recall your last five gifts — mark each one's engine honestly (guilt / pressure / transaction / grace-joy). Then make one gift today with the right engine: freely decided, zero compulsion, aimed at joy. Small is fine; cheerful is the point.
days.prayer: Lord, You love cheerful givers — so change what I find delightful. Strip out the guilt-engine and the deal-making. Give me the Macedonian equation: joy that overflows regardless of the balance, and giving I'd beg for the privilege of. Amen.
days.reflection: Which engine has driven most of your giving? What would have to change inside you for 'hilarious giver' to describe you?

days.t: The Tithe — Training Wheels of Trust

verse.text: Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house. And thereby put me to the test, says the LORD of hosts, if I will not open the windows of heaven for you and pour down for you a blessing until there is no more need.

days.teaching: The tithe — ten percent, first, to God's house — predates the Law (Abraham tithed to Melchizedek, Gen 14:20; Jacob vowed it at Bethel), structures it (Malachi calls withholding it robbery — 'you are robbing me... in your tithes and contributions'), and survives into Jesus' teaching (He affirmed tithing while indicting hearts that stopped there: 'these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others,' Matt 23:23). Whatever your theology of its New Covenant status — command or baseline — treat it functionally: the tithe is the training wheels of trust, the standing discipline that keeps God first in your cash flow (Day 4 of Rules of Money set the order; this day sets the floor), funds the local storehouse that feeds you spiritually (there may be food in my house — your church's ministry runs on somebody's obedience), and carries Scripture's only invited experiment: TEST ME in this. Practical honesty: most believers give far below a tithe, and the common objection — 'I can't afford it' — usually means the lifestyle was built first and God offered the remainder; the Malachi order builds God in first and sizes the lifestyle after. If ten percent from where you are is genuinely a cliff, take the staircase: name your current true percentage, step it up now, and schedule the next steps — but be moving, deliberately, toward and then past the floor. Grace-giving was never meant to be less than the Law's training wheels.
days.a: Compute your true number: last 12 months' giving ÷ last 12 months' income. Face it without flinching. Then set the Malachi structure: first-position automatic transfer to your church — at the tithe, or on a dated staircase toward it. Take the test formally; keep notes for 90 days.
days.prayer: LORD of hosts, You invited the test and I've been avoiding the math. Here's my true number, and here's my staircase. Be first in my cash flow, feed Your house through my hands, and open whatever windows You choose — I'll keep honest notes. Amen.
days.reflection: What was your true percentage — and what did you feel when you saw it? What lifestyle decision is actually competing with the tithe?

days.t: In Secret — Giving Without a Trumpet

verse.text: But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.

days.teaching: Jesus assumes His people give ('WHEN you give') and then attacks the ancient fundraising technology of the ego: the trumpet, the announcement, the plaque, the post. His diagnosis is brutal economics: applause-seeking givers 'have received their reward' — paid in full, in the currency they actually wanted; the transaction is complete and heaven owes nothing. Secret giving does surgery on the motive question Day 2 opened: with no audience, the only remaining reasons to give are love and the Father — which is why anonymous generosity feels different in the soul; it's the purest strain of the discipline. It also protects the receiver's dignity (charity with a spotlight makes the poor into props) and protects YOU from generosity's occupational disease: becoming the Benefactor, a persona that quietly converts every gift back into self. The hilarious mechanics of 'left hand not knowing': give fast and forget, keep no mental ledger of gratitude owed, let some gifts be unthanked forever. One tension to resolve honestly: Jesus also said 'let your light shine... that they may see your good works' (Matt 5:16) — the resolution is direction (visibility that glorifies the FATHER and models generosity for others can be right; visibility that collects credit for you never is). When in doubt: secret. The Father sees in secret, and His reward outlasts the plaque.
days.a: Execute one fully anonymous gift this week (plan it today): cash to a need, a bill paid through the church office, an unsigned envelope — genuinely untraceable to you. Tell no one, ever. Let it be between you and the One who sees in secret.
days.prayer: Father who sees in secret, I've enjoyed some trumpets. Teach me the anonymous art — gifts with no ledger, no plaque, no persona. Purify the motive until the secret ones are my favorites, and Your seeing is reward enough. Amen.
days.reflection: How much does being seen (or thanked) factor into your giving, honestly? What was different — in the planning and in your soul — about the anonymous gift?

verse.text: Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.

days.teaching: Scripture's concern for the poor is not a theme — it's a torrent: the gleaning laws building charity into the harvest's edges (Lev 19:9-10), 'you shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor' (Deut 15:11), the fast God chooses being 'to share your bread with the hungry' (Isa 58), Job's defense resting on it ('I was eyes to the blind... father to the needy'), Jesus inaugurating His ministry with 'good news to the poor' and identifying Himself with them so completely that Matthew 25 makes care for 'the least of these' the evidence read at judgment — 'as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.' Proverbs 19:17 adds the staggering banking metaphor: generosity to the poor is a LOAN TO GOD, personally guaranteed. Practice requires overcoming the modern distance problem — the poor have been zoned, screened, and algorithm'd out of most middle-class sightlines, so generosity needs deliberate proximity: know actual names (the widow in the congregation, the struggling family on the street, the refugee ministry's real people), give directly and through the church's benevolence (both — direct for proximity, structured for wisdom), and give helpfully (relief for crises; development for capacity — teaching, employing, and buying-from are generosity too; the goal is people restored, not dependencies installed). And keep Jesus' identification in front of you: at your gate, in distressing disguise, He waits.
days.a: Close the distance: identify by NAME one poor or struggling person/family within your actual reach (church, street, workplace). Make one direct provision this week (groceries, a bill, employment, a skill given) — and set up one recurring channel (church benevolence fund or trusted ministry).
days.prayer: Lord of the least of these, You wait at my gate in disguise. Give me eyes that stopped screening You out, proximity that costs me comfort, and a hand open wide by policy. I want to be found having lent much to You. Amen.
days.reflection: How has distance been organizing your compassion? Whose name did you learn — and what does 'lending to the LORD' change about the risk?

days.t: Hospitality — Generosity With a Front Door

verse.text: But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. You will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.

days.teaching: Jesus watched dinner-party economics — everyone inviting those who could reciprocate — and flipped the guest list: invite those who CANNOT repay, and collect at the resurrection. Hospitality is generosity's most embodied form: not entertaining (impressing peers with your table) but philoxenia — love of strangers — the open door commanded across both Testaments ('seek to show hospitality,' Rom 12:13; 'show hospitality to one another without grumbling,' 1 Pet 4:9 — Peter, realist, anticipating the grumbling; elders disqualified without it, 1 Tim 3:2). Your home is a generosity instrument possibly more powerful than your checkbook: a table seats the lonely (Ps 68:6's 'God settles the solitary in a home' usually uses somebody's actual home), the new family, the single parent and her kids, the international student who's never been inside an American house, the unbeliever who'll hear grace said over food before ever hearing a sermon. The barriers are almost all vanity in disguise: the house isn't nice enough (hospitality isn't a magazine shoot — soup and honesty beat catering and performance), the schedule's full (so is everyone's; the table happens by calendar, not by margin), it's awkward (awkward is the entry fee; ask the formerly-lonely if it was worth it). Jesus' resurrection-accounting stands over all of it: guest lists that can't repay you are deposits in the only bank that survives death.
days.a: Flip one guest list: plan a meal this month whose invitees CANNOT repay you socially — the lonely, the new, the struggling, the never-invited. Set the date today and send the first invitation. Soup is sufficient. Presence is the point.
days.prayer: Lord of the flipped guest list, You set a table for me when I had nothing to bring. Make my home an instrument — door open, soup on, resurrection accounting. Deliver me from entertaining, and teach me the love of strangers. Amen.
days.reflection: Who's been eating at your table — reciprocators, or Luke 14 guests? What vanity has kept the door shut, and who's on the flipped list?

days.t: The Widow's Two Coins — Proportion, Not Amount

verse.text: Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.

days.teaching: Jesus sat opposite the treasury and WATCHED how people gave — unsettling in itself — and then re-ranked the leaderboard: the widow's two lepta (worth almost nothing) counted as MORE than the large gifts, because heaven's accounting measures proportion and cost, not amount: 'they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty.' Two liberations and one challenge follow. Liberation one: small givers are not small givers — if resources are thin, your twenty dollars may outweigh a tycoon's twenty thousand on the only scoreboard that matters; give without embarrassment. Liberation two: the game is not rigged toward the rich — generosity is the most democratized discipline in the Kingdom. The challenge: for those NOT in the widow's poverty, the standard quietly inverts — if she gave everything from nothing, what does giving-out-of-abundance that never touches lifestyle actually cost? C.S. Lewis's rule lands here: 'the only safe rule is to give more than we can spare... if our charities do not at all pinch or hamper us, they are too small.' The question graduates from 'how much did I give?' to 'what did it cost me?' — did any comfort, upgrade, or plan actually yield? Sacrificial is the Bible's consistent adjective for praised giving (David: 'I will not offer... that which costs me nothing,' 2 Sam 24:24). Find your pinch point. That's where the widow's category begins.
days.a: Find the pinch: identify one real comfort, upgrade, or plan you could yield this season, and convert its cost into giving (the trip downsized, the upgrade skipped, the eating-out budget halved for a quarter). Make it specific, schedule the converted gift — and notice whether it pinches. It should.
days.prayer: Lord who watches the treasury, re-rank my giving by Your scoreboard. Free me from amount-embarrassment and abundance-comfort both. Show me my pinch point — and give me the widow's strange freedom: open hands all the way down. Amen.
days.reflection: Has your giving ever actually pinched? What did you find at the pinch point — and what does your resistance to it reveal?

days.t: Rich Toward God — the Portfolio Review

verse.text: Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail... For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

days.teaching: Jesus talks like an investment advisor with insider knowledge: provide YOURSELVES with moneybags that don't age, treasure that can't fail — giving reframed as the era's only non-depreciating asset class (the Investor's Path ended here on purpose; this day goes further). The mechanism is the famous heart-follows-treasure law: you don't give where your heart is — your heart migrates to where your treasure went (fund a missionary and watch yourself start praying for her; invest in the youth ministry and notice you now care about teenagers). Which makes giving a discipleship steering wheel: allocate treasure deliberately toward what you WANT to care about, and your affections will follow the money. Now run the portfolio review Jesus implies: pull your last twelve months of statements and read them as a heart-map — every dollar was a vote for where your heart would move; where has it been voting? Then rebalance like an investor: churches and works that gospel your city, the poor (Day 5's channels), the unreached (the going and the sending — 'no one who has left house or lands for my sake... will fail to receive a hundredfold,' Mark 10:29-30), the next generation's formation. And hear the 'sell your possessions' clause honestly: for the rich young ruler it was total (the possession owned him); for Zacchaeus, half, unprompted, with joy; for you — the command is at minimum this: nothing you own is exempt from the conversation. Hold the whole portfolio loosely enough that Jesus can reallocate any position.
days.a: Run the heart-map audit: print/pull 12 months of spending + giving. Mark where your treasure actually voted. Write the three-line finding ('my heart has been steered toward ___'). Then rebalance: one new deliberate kingdom allocation, sized to steer your heart where you want it to go.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, my statements are a map of my heart's migrations — I read them today without flinching. Take the portfolio: reallocate anything, exempt nothing. Steer my treasure toward Your kingdom until my heart has no choice but to follow. Amen.
days.reflection: What did the heart-map show — where has your treasure been steering you? Which position would be hardest for Jesus to reallocate, and why that one?

days.t: Generosity Beyond Money — Time, Skill, and Presence

verse.text: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace.

days.teaching: Money is generosity's most liquid currency but rarely its most costly: Peter's command covers 'God's VARIED grace' — every received gift converted to service. The fuller wallet: TIME (for the overscheduled, an afternoon may cost more than a check — and presence is the gift grief, loneliness, and childhood actually request; you cannot Venmo a hospital visit); SKILL (the accountant doing the widow's taxes, the mechanic fixing the single mom's car, the lawyer's pro bono hour, the tradesman teaching a fatherless teenager — skilled generosity often delivers 10x the value of its cash equivalent and dignifies both parties); ATTENTION (the full-eye-contact conversation in a distracted age is almost exotic); HOSPITALITY (Day 6); ADVOCACY (your network and credibility spent opening doors for people who lack both — 'open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute,' Prov 31:8); and honor's close cousin, ENCOURAGEMENT (Barnabas — 'son of encouragement' — got his NAME from giving it; his generosity launched Paul). The discipline mirrors money exactly: budget it (unscheduled time-generosity gets devoured by the urgent, like unscheduled savings), give it first-fruits (the fresh Saturday morning hour, not the exhausted remnant), and watch the same law hold — sown time, skill, and presence reap where money can't even plant.
days.a: Write your varied-grace inventory: list your top three non-money assets (skills, access, time blocks, encouragement). Assign each one a recipient and a date this month — the pro bono job, the taught skill, the standing visit. Book the first one today.
days.prayer: God of varied grace, I've outsourced my generosity to my wallet. Take the fuller inventory: my hours, my hands, my skills, my rooms, my voice. Budget them like money, spend them like seed — and make me a Barnabas to somebody this month. Amen.
days.reflection: Which is harder for you to give — money, time, or presence — and what does that difficulty locate? Who received skilled generosity from you last, and who's next?

verse.text: I have received full payment, and more. I am well supplied, having received from Epaphroditus the gifts you sent, a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God.

days.teaching: Hidden inside Philippians is generosity's neglected half: Paul — the tentmaker fiercely proud of self-support — RECEIVING, gratefully and publicly, and teaching the church how by example. He receives without groveling (no debtor's shame), names the gift's true nature (not charity to him but 'a fragrant offering... pleasing to GOD' — receiving well, he lets the givers' worship complete), and receives without letting the gift govern him. Why this day matters in a giving plan: chronic inability to receive is generosity's shadow disease — the person who always gives and never receives isn't humble but often proud (self-sufficiency wearing servant's clothes), and they quietly rob everyone around them of the blessing Jesus said was greater ('more blessed to give' — someone must receive for anyone to be blessed). Peter nearly made this mistake at the basin: 'You shall never wash my feet' — and Jesus' answer was severe: 'If I do not wash you, you have no share with me' (John 13:8). Receiving grace-fully is practice for the gospel itself, which cannot be earned, repaid, or politely declined — only received. So: accept the offered meal, the offered help, the offered gift, without the instant reciprocity reflex (immediate repayment is refusal with manners); say thank you and let it stand; ask for help when you need it (the mature move you've been calling weakness); and when God supplies through people, thank both. Givers who can't receive haven't finished learning generosity. Complete the circuit.
days.a: Practice the neglected half: (1) accept the next offer of help/generosity WITHOUT deflecting or instantly repaying — full stop at 'thank you'; (2) actually ask one person for help you genuinely need this week; (3) recall a gift you deflected recently — go back and receive it properly (tell them what it meant).
days.prayer: Lord, You let a sinful woman anoint Your feet and called it beautiful — and You warned Peter that refusing to receive refuses You. Heal my receiving. Break the self-sufficiency that robs other givers of their blessing, and make me gracious at both ends of the gift. Amen.
days.reflection: Why is receiving hard for you — pride, debt-fear, unworthiness? Who has been trying to give to you, and what has your deflection been costing them?

days.t: Sowing and the Supplier of Seed

verse.text: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.

days.teaching: Paul's giving chapter contains the doctrine that makes lifelong generosity sustainable: the SUPPLY LOOP. 'He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing' (v10) — God resupplies sowers; 'you will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way' (v11) — enrichment's stated purpose is further generosity. Read the loop precisely, because two errors wreck it. The prosperity error reads it as a vending machine: give to GET, wealth as the goal and God as the mechanism — but the text's every enrichment clause terminates in generosity, not lifestyle ('enriched... TO BE GENEROUS'); the harvest is 'the harvest of your righteousness,' and the guaranteed sufficiency is 'all sufficiency... for every good WORK' — seed for sowing, not seed for hoarding. The scarcity error refuses to believe resupply at all: it gives once, flinches, and returns to clutching — functionally atheist about verse 8. The sustainable middle is the farmer's faith: sow, trusting the Supplier; receive the resupply; sow again, larger; repeat for a lifetime — generosity as a flow you participate in rather than a stock you deplete. This is why generous people so often seem mysteriously resourced: not magic, but a loop — God routes supply through reliable distribution points, and open hands hold more traffic than closed ones. Your role is not to audit the loop's timing (resupply follows God's calendar, and some accounts settle at resurrection — Luke 14:14 stands). Your role is to stay a sower.
days.a: Test your loop-faith honestly: has a past gift's 'flinch' quietly shrunk your sowing? Name the flinch, then sow against it — repeat or exceed the gift that scared you, as a deliberate act of trust in the Supplier of seed.
days.prayer: Supplier of seed, I renounce both distortions: giving to get, and clutching in unbelief. Make me a distribution point in Your loop — sowing, resupplied, sowing larger — with sufficiency for every good work and my accounting left to You. Amen.
days.reflection: Which error tempts you — the vending machine or the clutch? Where have you seen the loop actually operate in your history, and what did it teach?

verse.text: And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, 'Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.' And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house.'

days.teaching: Nobody commanded Zacchaeus. One lunch with Jesus and the tax collector stands up mid-meal and reorganizes his entire net worth — half to the poor, fourfold restitution to the defrauded (exceeding the Law's requirement by multiples) — and Jesus reads the balance-sheet earthquake as diagnostic: 'TODAY salvation has come to this house.' Not that giving purchased salvation; that salvation, arrived, MOVES MONEY — the wallet being the last organ converted and the surest evidence when it is. This day holds two mirrors. Mirror one, restitution: Zacchaeus's generosity started with repair — money wrongly gained went back first, with interest; before expansive giving comes clean books (anything gained by the old thumb-on-scale — the unpaid debt, the padded claim, the borrowed-never-returned — restitution is generosity's foundation, and its power as testimony is nuclear: fourfold repayment made Jericho believe something had genuinely happened to their tax man). Mirror two, evidence: John the Baptist made generosity the repentance-fruit ('whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none,' Luke 3:11); James made withheld generosity the faith-falsifier (faith without works is dead, and his exhibit is a brother unfed); 1 John makes it the love-test ('if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him?'). The uncomfortable question the day asks plainly: does your money show that salvation came to your house? Not perfectly — directionally. Zacchaeus's direction changed at lunch. Yours can change at this one.
days.a: Do the Zacchaeus double: (1) restitution scan — anything wrongly gained or owing (money, property, credit)? Repair one item this week, generously; (2) evidence check — write what your last year's money movements would lead a neutral auditor to conclude happened (or didn't) in your house. Respond to the finding with one Zacchaeus-sized move.
days.prayer: Lord who invited Yourself to lunch, come sit over my books. Where the old life still owes, fund the restitution; where the evidence is thin, move the money until it testifies. Let it be said of my house: today salvation came — and the ledgers prove it. Amen.
days.reflection: What would the neutral auditor conclude from your money's movements? What restitution or evidence-move is your Zacchaeus moment?

verse.text: You shall give to him freely, and your heart shall not be grudging when you give to him, because for this the LORD your God will bless you in all your work and in all that you undertake.

days.teaching: One generation's generosity is a gift; transmitted generosity is a dynasty — and transmission doesn't happen by osmosis. The Deuteronomy pattern put giving inside the family's rhythms (tithes, gleaning edges, festival provisions for 'the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow' — children WATCHED the household economy include the vulnerable as policy, annually, physically). Build the modern equivalent deliberately: give VISIBLY inside the house even while giving secretly outside it (children can't imitate what they never see — let them watch the tithe get set apart first and hear why: 'this goes back to God before anything, because it's all His'); give THROUGH their hands (kids delivering the groceries, choosing the angel-tree gift, handling the giving-jar math — generosity learned through the body outlasts lectures); build the three-jar architecture early (give/save/spend — the whole Flourish wealth curriculum in preschool form); tell the family giving STORIES (the resupply-loop testimonies, the anonymous adventures — sanitized as needed; stories are how values ride down generations); and let them see the PINCH occasionally ('we're not doing X this year because we committed Y to the missionaries' — abundance-only generosity teaches that giving is a luxury feature, not a covenant practice). The stakes are generational: Proverbs 13:22's inheritance to children's children includes the treasury code (Rules of Money, Day 13) — and generosity is the code's crown jewel, the one that keeps wealth from curdling into entitlement in the third generation. Raise givers, not just heirs.
days.a: Install one transmission structure this week: the visible tithe moment, the three jars, the kids-hands delivery, or the family giving story at dinner. If your children are grown — tell them one giving story they've never heard, and propose one family gift decided together this year.
days.prayer: God of generations, let generosity outlive me in my house. Put the giving where my children can see it, in their hands where they can feel it, and in our stories where it can ride down the line. Raise givers from my table — heirs of open hands. Amen.
days.reflection: What did you learn about giving from watching your parents' money — and what are your children (or the young people watching you) currently learning from yours?

days.t: You Will Be Made Rich in Every Way — the Generous Life Entire

verse.text: In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'

days.teaching: Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders ends with the beatitude that summarizes this whole plan — MORE BLESSED TO GIVE — and his life credentials the claim: hands that worked to have something to give, a ministry spent, a self poured out 'as a drink offering.' Now assemble the Generous Life entire into its rule: the family resemblance settled (givers because He gave); the engine converted (cheerful, decided, free); the floor structured (tithe, first-position, automatic); the trumpet retired (secret gifts on the calendar); the gate attended (the poor by name, relief and development); the door open (Luke 14 guest lists, monthly); the pinch found (sacrifice as the standard, proportion as the measure); the portfolio steered (treasure ahead of heart, reviewed annually); the varied grace budgeted (time, skill, presence, advocacy); the circuit completed (receiving healed); the loop trusted (sow, resupply, sow larger); the books cleaned (restitution done, evidence visible); the house enrolled (givers raised, stories told). And over the whole rule, the final reframe: generosity is not a discipline you perform for God — it is participation in who He IS; every open-handed act joins the eternal current that flows from the Father of lights, 'who gives generously to all without reproach,' through the Son who 'though he was rich, yet for your sake became poor,' by the Spirit poured out — into you, and through you, and onward. The reservoir was never the plan. You were always meant to be a river. Open the gates, and stay open — the Supplier has never once run dry.
days.a: Write your Generosity Rule of Life: one page — percentages and staircase, secret-gift rhythm, poor-by-name channel, hospitality schedule, varied-grace commitments, family structures, annual portfolio review date. Sign it with your household. Then celebrate completion the plan's own way: one last gift today, purely for the joy of it.
days.prayer: Father of lights, Son who became poor, Spirit poured out — make me a river in Your current. Seal this rule into decades: cheerful, secret, sacrificial, proportional, transmitted, and trusting the resupply. More blessed to give — let my whole life test and prove it. Amen.
days.reflection: Which day of this plan rearranged you most? A decade from now, what should be true of your church, your city, and your children because this rule was kept?

plans.title: 21-Day Marriage Renewal
plans.tagline: Covenant is courtship continued. Re-pursue, repair, and rebuild — starting today.
plans.promise: Twenty-one days of deliberate pursuit: deeper conversation, faster repair, restored affection, and shared prayer. Marriages drift by default and deepen by design.

days.a: Read your vows (or Genesis 2) and write one paragraph: what did I promise, and where have I been coasting? Diagnosis with grace — for you, not against them.

verse.text: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.

days.teaching: The first institution: leave, cleave, become one. Oneness requires a prior leaving. And the nakedness without shame is the signature of a covenant kept — intimacy has no fear where there is no hiddenness.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'The Covenant Re-Read' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Live with your wife in an understanding way — the word implies study. Today, ask your spouse: 'What's been heaviest for you this month?' Then only listen. No fixing.

verse.text: Husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor.

days.teaching: The peacemaker carries an authority the argumentative never touch. By year three, your communities should know you as the man who can stand between parties without picking up either one's offense: the brothers feuding, the church factions, the family cold war. The mediator's tools are simple and rare — hear both fully, name truth without venom, propose the smallest next step toward repair, and absorb some cost yourself to make peace cheaper for everyone else. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God — the family resemblance is the point.
days.prayer: Lord, renew my covenant pursuit. Give me the energy of the man who first won her — the planned pursuit, the studied attention, the quick repair. Make me a scholar of my wife and a servant of my house. In Jesus' name, amen.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'The Study Begins' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Praise your spouse specifically in front of someone else today — kids, friends, parents. Honor delivered in public pays double.

verse.text: Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her: 'Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all.'

days.teaching: The fruit of an excellent wife is the blessing of those nearest her — her children and her husband. The praise rises from those who know her best. A life well-lived is honored first in the home.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'Public Praise' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Settle the oldest small offense currently open between you. Do not let the sun go down — apologize for your side without a 'but.'

verse.text: Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger...

days.teaching: Your mind is the control center of your life. Every decision, every relationship, every financial choice flows through your thought patterns. The Bible commands you to 'take every thought captive'—not because God is controlling, but because He knows the damage an undisciplined mind can cause. The modern man is bombarded with more information in a single day than his grandfather processed in a month. Screens, notifications, pornography, clickbait, political outrage—all of it competes for the same limited mental real estate. Without discipline, your mind becomes a rental property occupied by whoever pays the highest attention bid.
days.prayer: Lord, my thoughts feel like a battlefield. Anxieties attack from one side, temptations from another, and distractions from every direction. I need Your peace to guard my mind. Help me identify the thoughts that do not belong and replace them with truth. Give me the discipline to feed my mind what is pure, noble, and right. Let my mental clarity honor You. In Jesus' name, amen.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'The Quick Repair' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Affection with no destination: the long hug, held hand, shoulder rub. Today affection is a gift, not a request.

verse.text: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me!

days.teaching: The image is tender and resting — the beloved held and at peace. Intimacy in marriage includes the quiet embrace, the presence without performance. Love is not only passion; it is shelter.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'Touch Without Agenda' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Come, let us go out into the fields — plan a real date for this week: calendar, sitter if needed, phones off, one new question prepared.

verse.text: Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the fields and lodge in the villages; let us go out early to the vineyards and see whether the vines have budded...

days.teaching: The bride invites her beloved to go away together — to journey, to lodge, to see the vines. Marital love thrives on intentional time, on getting away together. The vineyard is the place of both fruit and fellowship.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'The Date Architecture' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Rest together deliberately: a slow meal, a walk, no logistics talk. Come away by yourselves — rest is a couple's discipline too.

verse.text: And he said to them, Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.

days.teaching: You do not need a gym membership to be fit. You need a protocol. A simple, repeatable structure. For men, I recommend a weekly split: Day 1—Upper Body Push (push-ups, dips, overhead press). Day 2—Lower Body (squats, lunges, deadlifts). Day 3—Upper Body Pull (pull-ups, rows, curls). Day 4—Active Recovery (walk, mobility, light cardio). Repeat. Three to four sets of 8-12 reps per exercise. Add weight progressively. If you have no equipment, start with bodyweight. The goal is not to become a bodybuilder. The goal is functional strength, mental clarity, and the discipline that carries into every other area of life.
days.prayer: God, I praise You for the body You have given me. It is fearfully and wonderfully made, even in its imperfections. Help me care for it as a gift, not a burden. Give me the discipline to move it, fuel it properly, and rest it adequately. Let my physical health be a testimony of good stewardship. In Jesus' name, amen.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'Sabbath Together' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Pray aloud together for two minutes tonight — thanks, one request each, done. Awkward is fine. Agreement is built by repetition, not eloquence.

verse.text: Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them.

days.teaching: Agreement in prayer carries unique authority. Christ is present where His name is gathered. United prayer is not louder prayer; it is prayer that has aligned with another and therefore with the Father's will.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'First Shared Prayer' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Gracious words are honeycomb. Send three specific encouraging texts to your spouse across the day. Specific beats sweet.

verse.text: Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body.

days.teaching: Business is simply solving problems for profit. The man who identifies a pain point and creates a solution will never lack income. But business also requires systems. You need a way to attract customers (marketing), a way to convert them (sales), a way to deliver (operations), and a way to keep them (retention). Each of these is a skill that can be learned. Read 'The E-Myth Revisited' for systems thinking. Read ' $100 Startup' for low-capital models. Then execute. Reading without action is entertainment, not education.
days.prayer: God, thank You for the ability to work and earn. I do not take it for granted. Help me maximize my earning potential without sacrificing my character. Give me creative ideas, productive systems, and favor with clients and employers. Let my work be excellent, my word be trusted, and my prices be fair. In Jesus' name, amen.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'The Encouragement Flood' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: One hour, no screens: 'What dreams have you shelved? What do you want the next five years to look like?' Quick to hear, slow to speak — your only job is to understand.

verse.text: Be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger.

days.teaching: Spiritual sons are raised at your side, not recruited from a stage. Year three asks every man: who is your Timothy? Find the younger man with hunger in his eyes and invite him into your actual life — the workshop, the workout, the budget review, the prayer closet. Structure helps: a book read together, a weekly question, a project shared. But the curriculum is mostly you, observed up close, including your repentance. One man raised well outweighs a hundred impressed from a distance. Paul's letters survive because Paul's Timothys did.
days.prayer: Father, forge my character in the fire and let it hold. Make my word my bond, my tongue a builder, and my integrity my children's inheritance. When the test comes with a cost attached, find me already decided. In Jesus' name, amen.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'The Listening Hour' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Do the chore or errand they hate most, unasked and unannounced. Count others more significant — covenant love does recon.

verse.text: Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.

days.teaching: Humility is not thinking less of yourself; it is counting others more significant. The command is active: look to the interests of another. Love is the effort of turning the eye outward.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'Serve the Unspoken' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Execute the date. Dress like it matters. Ask the prepared question. End with gratitude spoken aloud for one specific thing about them.

verse.text: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine,

days.teaching: The Song begins with desire — honest, embodied, covenantal. Love in marriage is to be desired and celebrated, not merely endured. The bride speaks her longing without shame because the covenant has made it safe.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'The Date' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Privately list any resentments you're still holding. Forgive each before God by name — as the Lord has forgiven you. Decide which one conversation would help, and schedule it gently.

verse.text: bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.

days.teaching: Forgiveness is not optional for those who have been forgiven. The standard is not what the other deserves but what you received. To withhold forgiveness after receiving it is to forget the cost of your own pardon.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'Forgiveness Inventory' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days. Rest together and talk about one happy memory per year you've been together. Memory is marriage fuel.

verse.text: Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your fleeting life that he has given you under the sun, because that is your portion in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.

days.teaching: Marriage is a gift to be enjoyed, not a burden to be endured. The Preacher calls life fleeting and then calls you to enjoy your wife all your days. Joy in the ordinary covenant is your God-given portion.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'Sabbath — The Long View' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.

days.a: I have made a covenant with my eyes. Audit your inputs — shows, feeds, follows — and remove anything that erodes desire for your actual spouse. Tell them you did it and why.

verse.text: I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?

days.teaching: Purity begins with a covenant of the eye. Job did not wait for temptation; he pre-decided. The covenant is made before the glance, because the glance is where the battle is won or lost.
days.reflection: Where in your life this week is 'Guard the Gates' most needed? Take the action honestly and note what you learn.
